scenarios.title: Planning Your Study Path
scenarios.situation: You have 3 weeks before your DevOps: Zero to Hire interview/exam. You've just opened this bootcamp with 15 domains ahead of you.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most effective study sequence?
choices: Start Here lessons → core domains in order → Systems Anatomy → Mock Assessment → Capstone, doing drills daily
Jump straight to the Mock Assessment to see where you stand
Study only your weakest domain until it's perfect, then move on
Read all lessons first, then do all scenarios, then all labs
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The bootcamp is sequenced deliberately: orientation first, then progressive domain mastery with interleaved drills for retention, Systems Anatomy to connect it all, mock under realistic conditions, capstone to prove it. Jumping to the mock wastes its diagnostic value; perfecting one domain starves the others; batching by activity type kills interleaving benefits.
scenarios.hint: What does each phase prepare you for? What happens if you skip the foundation?

scenarios.title: The Passive Reader Trap
scenarios.situation: A learner has 'completed' 40 lessons but fails every scenario. They read each lesson carefully and passed all knowledge checks on the first try.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what's the fix?
choices: They consumed passively without application — the fix is interleaving scenarios immediately after lessons and doing teach-backs aloud
The lessons are too easy — skip to harder material
They need to re-read the lessons more carefully
Knowledge checks are broken — report a bug
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Passing knowledge checks proves recognition, not application. Scenarios demand transfer — using knowledge in novel situations. The fix is structural: never finish a lesson without immediately attempting its scenarios, and explain each concept aloud (teach-back) to expose shallow understanding.
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between recognizing an answer and producing one under pressure?

scenarios.title: Which skill first?
scenarios.situation: You're starting from help-desk experience and want a DevOps role. You have four hours a day to study. The internet says learn Kubernetes, Terraform, Python, AWS, Docker, and Jenkins all at once, and you're paralyzed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage learning order?
evidence: 2 years help desk: Windows troubleshooting, ticket queues, basic networking
choices: Linux fundamentals first, then Git, then containers (Docker), then CI/CD basics, then cloud and IaC — each layer compounds on the previous one.
Start with Kubernetes — it's what job postings mention most, so learn the hardest thing first.
Learn all six in parallel, one hour each per day, to stay balanced.
Skip Linux and Git — they're old technologies and the cloud abstracts them away.
scenarios.why: DevOps skills stack: you can't debug a container without Linux, can't collaborate without Git, and can't understand Kubernetes without containers. Sequential depth beats parallel breadth — each layer makes the next one learnable. Job-posting keywords without foundations produce candidates who can't troubleshoot.
scenarios.hint: Every advanced tool assumes the layer below it. Which layer does everything else stand on?

scenarios.title: The portfolio with no proof
scenarios.situation: Your resume lists Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, and AWS, but every project is a tutorial you followed click-for-click. In a phone screen, you're asked to describe something you built and you freeze.
scenarios.prompt: What portfolio change makes you hirable?
evidence: Projects: Docker tutorial app, K8s guestbook tutorial, Terraform EC2 tutorial
choices: Build one end-to-end project of your own design (e.g. a small app with CI pipeline, container build, IaC deployment, and monitoring) and document your decisions in the repo README.
Add more tutorial projects to the resume so the skills list looks longer.
Remove the projects section — tutorials look worse than nothing.
Copy a senior engineer's portfolio project and present it as your own.
scenarios.why: Hiring managers probe for decisions, trade-offs, and debugging stories — tutorials have none because someone else made the choices. One original end-to-end project demonstrates you can integrate tools and explain why, which is what interviews actually test.
scenarios.hint: Interviewers don't ask what you typed — they ask why you chose it and what broke. Which project gives you those stories?

scenarios.title: The take-home pipeline
scenarios.situation: A take-home assignment asks you to containerize a Python API, add CI that runs tests, and deploy it somewhere. You have a weekend. You're tempted to hand-roll everything to look impressive.
scenarios.prompt: What approach best demonstrates DevOps judgment?
evidence:
Containerize API, CI runs tests, deploy somewhere accessible
Timebox: one weekend
choices: Use boring, standard tooling (Dockerfile, GitHub Actions, a managed platform or simple IaC), keep it working end-to-end, and write a short README covering what you'd do with more time.
Build a custom CI system from scratch to show deep knowledge.
Deploy to a Kubernetes cluster you build by hand to prove you can.
Skip tests in CI — the assignment is about deployment, not testing.
scenarios.why: Take-homes evaluate judgment under constraints: a working, maintainable, well-documented standard stack beats an impressive-but-fragile custom build. The README's 'with more time' section shows you know what production-hardening looks like without gold-plating a weekend project. Skipping tests signals you don't value the pipeline's purpose.
scenarios.hint: The reviewer has 20 minutes. What impresses more: exotic tooling that barely works, or a clean standard pipeline with honest documentation?

scenarios.title: The 'tell me about a failure' question
scenarios.situation: In an interview you're asked: 'Tell me about a time you caused an outage.' Your instinct is to pick a tiny, blameless story to look safe.
scenarios.prompt: How should you answer?
evidence: Round 3: behavioral. Interviewer: 'Tell me about a time you caused an outage.'
choices: Tell a real story with the STAR structure: what broke, your role, how you responded, and the systemic fix you implemented so it can't recur — showing ownership and learning.
Say you've never caused an outage — it shows you're careful.
Blame the tooling and the on-call rotation for the incident.
Give a vague answer without specifics to avoid looking bad.
scenarios.why: Interviewers ask about failure to assess ownership, incident response, and whether you fix systems or just symptoms. A real story ending in a systemic prevention (runbook, guardrail, test) demonstrates senior thinking. Claiming perfection is unbelievable; blame and vagueness signal the opposite of what DevOps culture values.
scenarios.hint: The question isn't testing whether you fail — everyone does. What is it actually testing?

scenarios.title: The salary question trap
scenarios.situation: A recruiter asks for your current salary early in the process. You're underpaid at $65k and the role is budgeted far higher. You worry that answering honestly anchors you low, but refusing feels adversarial.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best response?
evidence: Recruiter: 'So we can align on comp — what's your current salary?'
choices: Deflect to expectations: share your target range based on market research for the role and location, and note that in many jurisdictions employers can't ask for salary history — keep the conversation on the role's value.
State your current $65k honestly — honesty is always the best policy.
Inflate your current salary to $110k so the offer anchors higher.
Refuse to discuss compensation at all until an offer is on the table.
scenarios.why: Compensation should anchor to the role's market value, not your history — that's why many places restrict salary-history questions. A researched target range keeps you collaborative while protecting your leverage. Lying about salary is discoverable and disqualifying; total refusal stalls the process unnecessarily.
scenarios.hint: The negotiation is about what the role is worth, not what you used to make. How do you move the anchor to the role?

scenarios.title: Two offers, different growth
scenarios.situation: Offer A: $115k at a large enterprise, maintaining legacy Jenkins and VMs, stable team, slow promotion. Offer B: $95k at a 40-person startup, building Kubernetes platform and GitOps from scratch, reporting to the CTO, steep learning curve.
scenarios.prompt: How should you evaluate the trade-off?
evidence:
A: $115k enterprise, legacy stack maintenance, slow growth
B: $95k startup, greenfield platform, CTO mentorship, high risk
choices: Weigh total career value, not just salary: estimate the skills, scope, and mentorship each role builds over 2-3 years against financial needs and risk tolerance — early career usually compounds faster on scope and learning.
Always take the higher salary — compensation is the only objective measure.
Always take the startup — enterprises never teach anything useful.
Decide by title prestige alone; the higher title wins.
scenarios.why: Early-career compensation is a fraction of lifetime earnings; the skills and scope you build compound far more. That doesn't mean always picking the startup — financial obligations and risk tolerance are real constraints — but the decision framework is total career value over a multi-year horizon, not first-year salary alone.
scenarios.hint: You're choosing what you'll be qualified for in three years, not just what you earn this year. Which choice builds the more valuable next version of you?

scenarios.title: CI Is Not CD
scenarios.situation: The team's 'CI/CD' builds on every push and then someone manually copies artifacts to production over SSH on Fridays.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct pipeline shape?
evidence: build on push; deploy = manual scp on Friday
2 Friday deploys broke prod this quarter
choices: CI (build + test on every change) feeding CD (automated, repeatable promotion through environments with gates) — every commit becomes a releasable artifact and deploys are boring, frequent, and reversible
CI and CD are synonyms; the Friday process just needs a checklist
Automate the scp in a script; that counts as CD
Deploy less often (monthly) to reduce Friday risk
scenarios.why: CI proves every change builds and passes tests; CD makes releases routine through automated promotion and deployment strategies. Manual Friday scp is the absence of CD — automating the artifact copy without gates just ships breakage faster.
scenarios.hint: Which part proves the change is good, and which part ships it safely?

scenarios.title: The Workflow That Runs Everything Twice
scenarios.situation: A GitHub Actions workflow triggers on both `push` and `pull_request` to main, so every PR runs the full test suite twice — burning 40 minutes of runner time per PR.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct trigger design?
evidence: duplicate runs on every PR from a branch
choices: Scope triggers: `on: pull_request` for PR validation and `on: push: branches: [main]` for post-merge — or use path filters / concurrency groups to cancel superseded runs
Delete the pull_request trigger; push covers PRs
Buy bigger runners; the duplication is unavoidable
Split into two workflows with identical jobs; duplication is fine
scenarios.why: push fires on the branch push and pull_request fires on the PR event — for PRs from the same repo you get both. Scoping push to main (post-merge) plus pull_request (pre-merge) eliminates the double-run; concurrency groups cancel stale runs.
scenarios.hint: Which events fire for a PR opened from a repo branch?

scenarios.title: Jenkinsfile in the Wrong Place
scenarios.situation: A Declarative Pipeline fails with `No such DSL method` on a plain `sh` step inside a `script` block — and secrets are hardcoded in the Jenkinsfile.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct Jenkins practice?
evidence: pipeline { agent any; stages { stage('x') { steps { script { sh '...' } } } } }
AWS keys committed in the Jenkinsfile
choices: Keep `sh` inside `steps` (it IS a valid step — the error means a typo or wrong context), move credentials to the credentials store referenced via `withCredentials`, and prefer shared libraries over copy-pasted stages
Declarative pipelines can't run shell; switch everything to Freestyle jobs
Commit the keys; private repos are safe storage
Put the whole pipeline in a `script {}` block; Declarative is optional
scenarios.why: `sh` is a core Declarative step — 'no such DSL method' points at a typo or calling it outside steps. Credentials belong in Jenkins' encrypted store (withCredentials binding), never in the repo. Shared libraries deduplicate pipeline logic across repos.
scenarios.hint: Where do secrets live: in the repo, or in the controller's store?

scenarios.title: RED, Not Just CPU
scenarios.situation: The team monitors CPU and memory but was blindsided by a checkout slowdown — the servers looked healthy while users suffered.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct service monitoring?
evidence: CPU 40%, memory 60% — all green during the incident
choices: Instrument RED metrics (Rate, Errors, Duration) per service in Prometheus and alert on them — resource metrics describe machines; RED describes the user experience; add USE for the underlying resources
Lower the CPU alert threshold to 30%; tighter machine alerts catch app issues
Monitor only uptime; latency is a product concern
Add more Grafana dashboards with the same CPU graphs
scenarios.why: RED (request rate, error rate, duration) measures what users feel; machine metrics measure what machines do. The incident was invisible to CPU monitoring by construction. USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) covers the resource layer beneath.
scenarios.hint: Which metrics would have been red while CPU was green?

scenarios.title: Blue-Green vs Canary at 3 AM
scenarios.situation: A risky database migration ships with the release. The team must choose a deployment strategy that can roll back in under a minute if the migration misbehaves.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct strategy choice?
choices: Blue-green: run the new version (green) alongside current (blue), validate against production traffic shadow or smoke tests, then flip the router — rollback is an instant flip back; canary's gradual ramp is slower to fully revert
Canary: ramp 1% → 100%; gradual is always safer regardless of rollback time
Rolling update: simplest, and rollback just reverses it
Recreate: fastest deploy, downtime is acceptable at 3 AM
scenarios.why: Blue-green keeps the old version warm behind the router — rollback is a single route flip, meeting the 60s constraint. Canary limits blast radius during ramp but full rollback takes the whole ramp in reverse. The migration risk argues for instant reversibility.
scenarios.hint: Which strategy keeps the old version warm and one flip away?

scenarios.title: On-Call Without the Burnout
scenarios.situation: The new hire joins a rotation where every alert pages, there's no runbook, and the same disk-full page fired 14 times last month.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct on-call hygiene?
evidence: none; knowledge in one senior's head
choices: Tune alerting (page only on user-impacting, actionable symptoms; ticket the rest), write runbooks for every page, and fix the top repeat offender each sprint — toil reduction is the job, not heroics
Page more people per alert; shared pain is fair
Mute the disk alert; disks always fill eventually
On-call is inherently miserable; endurance is the skill
scenarios.why: Google's SRE doctrine: pages must be actionable, urgent, and user-impacting — everything else is a ticket. Runbooks make response repeatable; eliminating toil (the 14x disk page → auto-remediation or capacity fix) is the durable improvement. Alert fatigue causes missed real pages.
scenarios.hint: What makes a page worth waking someone for?

scenarios.title: The Flaky Pipeline
scenarios.situation: The main pipeline fails ~30% of runs on the integration test stage. Developers have started merging with red builds 'because it's probably flaky.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response to flaky tests in a blocking pipeline?
choices: Quarantine immediately: tag flaky tests non-blocking, move to nightly informational runs, fix-or-delete within a sprint — a red build everyone ignores is worse than no gate
Increase retries to 5 — flakes pass eventually
Make integration tests non-blocking permanently — speed matters more

lessons.title: DevOps Career Path — Core concepts
concepts: Learn in dependency order: Linux, then Git, then containers, then CI/CD, then cloud and IaC — each layer makes the next one comprehensible, and skipping layers produces fragile knowledge.
DevOps is a toolchain plus a culture: automation, measurement, and sharing matter as much as the tools — interviews probe how you collaborate and respond to failure, not just syntax.
One original end-to-end project beats ten tutorials: build something of your own design, document your decisions, and collect debugging stories — that's what interviews mine.
The pipeline is the product: CI that builds, tests, scans, and deploys is the core DevOps artifact — be able to whiteboard one for any stack.
Behavioral interviews test ownership: prepare real failure stories in STAR format that end with a systemic fix, not just a recovery.
Negotiate on the role's market value with researched ranges — anchoring to salary history undervalues you, and many jurisdictions restrict those questions.

example.code:
git log --oneline --graph -8
docker build -t myapp:ci .
docker run --rm myapp:ci pytest
example.walkthrough: Review recent history, build the container image tagged for CI, and run the test suite inside the exact image that would ship. This is the smallest meaningful pipeline loop: build once, test the artifact, and only then promote it.

pitfalls: Common trap: collecting tool keywords without foundations — you can't troubleshoot Kubernetes if you can't read Linux logs.
Common trap: tutorial-only portfolio — interviewers ask about decisions and failures, which tutorials never give you.
Common trap: gold-plating take-homes with exotic tooling — boring, working, and documented wins.
Common trap: anchoring salary talks to current pay — research the role's market range instead.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Devops Zero To Hire move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence

Scenarios in this bootcamp mirror real incidents and decisions — the same shape as interview questions and exam case studies.

lessons.title: Study Strategy: How to Master This Material
concepts: Active recall beats re-reading: after each lesson, close it and write down the 3 key ideas from memory before checking.

Error-driven learning: every wrong scenario answer creates a drill card. Do your drills daily — they're personalized to your gaps.
Teach-back method: after each capstone milestone, explain what you built to someone (or a rubber duck) — gaps in your explanation are gaps in understanding.
Mock assessment protocol: take it timed, closed-book, in one sitting. Review every miss. Re-take after 48 hours.

lessons.title: Capstone: DevOps Portfolio Pipeline — Project Brief
concepts: Your capstone: a production-grade CI/CD pipeline deploying a real app with IaC and monitoring
Why a capstone matters: interviewers remember stories about things you built far longer than quiz scores. This is your proof.
Build in public: commit early, commit often. A git history showing iterative progress impresses more than a perfect final upload.
Document as you go: every decision gets a one-line reason in the README. Future-you (and interviewers) will thank present-you.
Scope discipline: a finished small project beats an abandoned ambitious one. The milestones below are sized to complete.
Demo readiness: you must be able to screen-share this project and narrate every part in under 5 minutes.

example.code:
DevOps Portfolio Pipeline — Milestones:

  1. App containerization & repo setup
  2. CI pipeline with tests & security scans
  3. IaC-provisioned staging environment
  4. CD to production with monitoring & alerting

Each milestone is independently demoable.
Finish one before starting the next.
example.walkthrough: Create your project repo today — even if it's just a README with the milestone list. Momentum starts with the first commit.

pitfalls: Gold-plating milestone 1 while milestones 4-5 remain untouched — timebox each milestone.
Building without documenting — an undocumented project is nearly worthless as a portfolio piece.
Waiting until it's 'ready' to commit — commit the skeleton now; iterate in the open.
lessons.try_it: Create the repo and README for DevOps Portfolio Pipeline now. Write the milestone list and your 'why' for each.

lessons.title: Capstone: DevOps Portfolio Pipeline — Build Guide
concepts: Milestone 1 — Foundation: scaffold the project, verify the toolchain works end-to-end before adding complexity.
Milestone 2 — Core: implement the central functionality. This is the demoable heart of the project.
Milestone 3 — Hardening: handle errors, add validation, make it robust enough to demo without fear.
Milestone 4 — Polish: README, diagrams, clean output. This is what separates 'homework' from 'portfolio'.
Testing each milestone: define 'done' as a verifiable behavior, not a feeling. Write the check before the code.
Narrative prep: for each milestone, prepare a 60-second explanation — what it does, why it matters, what was hard.

example.code:
Definition of done (example, Milestone 2):

  ✓ Core feature works with valid input
  ✓ Graceful error on invalid input
  ✓ Output verified against expected result
  ✓ Committed with a clear message
  ✓ README section updated

No milestone is done until all boxes check.
example.walkthrough: Work milestone 1 today. When every 'done' box checks, commit and move on. Resist the urge to perfect.

pitfalls: Skipping the hardening milestone — demos fail live, and robustness is what interviewers probe.
No verifiable 'done' criteria — 'it works on my machine' is not done.
Building all milestones before testing any — integrate and verify incrementally.
lessons.try_it: Complete milestone 1 of your capstone. Verify every 'done' box before moving on.

lessons.title: Capstone: DevOps Portfolio Pipeline — Demo & Interview Prep
concepts: The 5-minute demo arc: problem (30s) → approach (60s) → live walkthrough (2.5min) → lessons learned (60s).
Anticipate the deep questions: 'Why did you choose X over Y?' 'What breaks at scale?' 'What would you do differently?'
Resume bullet formula: Action verb + what you built + tech + measurable outcome. Quantify everything you can.
LinkedIn/portfolio: screenshots or a 60-second screen recording outperform text descriptions 10:1.
Bring the repo to interviews: offer to walk through the code. Few candidates do this — it signals genuine ownership.
Post-mortem: write 5 lines on what you'd improve. Interviewers love candidates who can critique their own work.

example.code:
Resume bullet:
  'Built {proj} processing [N] records with [tech];
   reduced [metric] by [X]% via [technique].'

Demo opener:
  'The problem: [one sentence].
   My approach: [one sentence].
   Let me show you...'
example.walkthrough: Draft your resume bullet and demo opener now, even before the project is done. They'll sharpen as you build.

pitfalls: Demoing without a narrative — clicking around silently while the interviewer watches is painful.
No answer for 'what would you do differently' — always have one; it shows growth mindset.
Portfolio link rot — verify every link on your resume actually works before submitting.
lessons.try_it: Record a 60-second screen share of your current progress. Watch it back — is the narrative clear?

lessons.title: Linux Shell Fluency
concepts: The shell is your primary interface to servers: pipes (|), redirection (>, >>), and globbing (*.log) compose small tools into pipelines
SSH is how you reach remote machines: key-based auth (never passwords), config files for hosts, tmux/screen for persistence
Permissions (rwx, chmod, chown) and ownership explain 80% of 'it works locally but not on the server'
Systemd manages services: systemctl status/start/enable, journalctl for logs — know these cold

example.code:
$ ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 user@server
$ journalctl -u nginx --since '1 hour ago' | grep -i error
$ chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519  # keys must not be group-readable
example.walkthrough: In the terminal: SSH config walkthrough, check a service status, tail its logs, fix a permission issue.

pitfalls: chmod 777 as a 'fix' — you've created a security hole, not a solution
Running everything as root instead of learning sudo scoping
No tmux on long-running remote work — connection drops kill your session
lessons.try_it: Set up SSH key auth to a practice host. Configure ~/.ssh/config with an alias.

lessons.title: Git: Beyond Commit & Push
concepts: Branches are cheap pointers; the power is in workflow: feature branches, rebasing vs merging, and clean history
Rebase keeps history linear and reviewable; merge preserves truth — know when each is appropriate
.gitignore, hooks, and aliases prevent entire classes of mistakes (committed secrets, broken builds)
git bisect finds the breaking commit via binary search — the fastest way to find regressions

example.code:
$ git checkout -b feature/x
$ git rebase main          # linear history
$ git bisect start; git bisect bad; git bisect good v1.2.0
example.walkthrough: Create a feature branch, make 3 commits, rebase onto main, and resolve a conflict. Then bisect a planted bug.

pitfalls: Committing secrets then 'removing' them — they're in history forever; rotate the credential
Force-pushing shared branches — rewriting colleagues' history
Huge monolithic commits — unreviewable; commit logically grouped changes
lessons.try_it: Configure a pre-commit hook that blocks commits containing 'password' or AWS key patterns.

lessons.title: Pipeline Anatomy: Build, Test, Deploy
concepts: A pipeline is stages (build → test → deploy) with gates between them — each gate is an automated quality decision
Fail fast: run quick checks (lint, unit) before slow ones (integration, e2e) — don't burn 20 min to learn about a typo
Artifacts flow forward: build once, promote the same binary through environments — never rebuild per environment
Pipeline-as-code (YAML in repo) means pipelines are reviewed, versioned, and reproducible like any code

example.code:
stages: [lint, unit-test, build, integration-test, deploy-staging, e2e, deploy-prod]
# gates: each stage must pass; deploy-prod needs manual approval
example.walkthrough: Sketch a pipeline for a web app: list stages, what each validates, and where the gates are.

pitfalls: Rebuilding artifacts per environment — 'works in staging' means nothing if prod got a different build
No manual gate before production — full auto-deploy without a human checkpoint is brave until it isn't
Secrets in pipeline YAML — use the CI system's secret store, never plaintext
lessons.try_it: Write a minimal pipeline YAML (any CI syntax) with 4 stages and one manual approval gate.

lessons.title: Testing Strategy for Pipelines
concepts: Test pyramid: many unit, fewer integration, few e2e — inverted pyramids are slow and flaky
Flaky tests erode trust: quarantine them immediately, fix or delete — a red build everyone ignores is worse than no tests
Contract tests protect service boundaries without spinning up the whole world
Coverage is a floor, not a goal: 80% with meaningful assertions beats 100% of assert-true

example.code:
# quarantine flaky: tag and exclude from blocking
# pytest -m 'not flaky'  (blocking)
# pytest -m flaky         (nightly, informational)
example.walkthrough: Categorize a test suite into pyramid layers. Identify the flakiest test and write its quarantine plan.

pitfalls: E2E-only suites — 45-minute pipelines that everyone bypasses
Testing implementation details — refactor breaks tests that should still pass
No test data strategy — tests fighting over shared state
lessons.try_it: Add one contract test between two services you know. Define the shared expectation explicitly.

lessons.title: Docker in Depth for DevOps
concepts: Images are layered filesystems + metadata; containers are running instances with isolated namespaces — images are templates, containers are processes
Multi-stage builds separate build-time deps from runtime — smaller, faster, more secure images
Registries version and distribute images; tags are mutable pointers — pin digests for production
The Dockerfile is a build script: order layers by change frequency for cache efficiency

example.code:
FROM node:20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
FROM node:20-alpine
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]
example.walkthrough: Write a multi-stage Dockerfile for a sample app. Compare image sizes: single-stage vs multi-stage.

pitfalls: Running as root in production containers — add USER directives
COPY . . before dependency install — cache invalidation on every code change
:latest in production — non-reproducible deploys
lessons.try_it: Harden a Dockerfile: non-root user, pinned base digest, .dockerignore, and no secrets in layers.

lessons.title: Kubernetes Core Objects
concepts: Pods are the atomic unit (one or more containers sharing network/storage); Deployments manage ReplicaSets manage Pods — know the hierarchy
Services provide stable networking to ephemeral pods: ClusterIP (internal), NodePort, LoadBalancer, Ingress (HTTP routing)
ConfigMaps/Secrets decouple config from images — twelve-factor apps read config from the environment
kubectl is your lens: get, describe, logs, exec — describe tells you WHY, logs tell you WHAT

example.code:
$ kubectl get pods -o wide
$ kubectl describe pod <name>   # events reveal scheduling failures
$ kubectl logs -f deployment/api --tail=100
example.walkthrough: Deploy a 2-replica nginx. Expose it via Service. Break it (bad image) and use describe to diagnose.

pitfalls: Editing live objects with kubectl edit — drift from git; use declarative YAML
No resource requests/limits — noisy neighbors and OOM kills
Secrets in plaintext YAML committed to git — use sealed secrets or external stores
lessons.try_it: Write Deployment + Service YAML from scratch. Apply, verify endpoints, then scale to 3.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Kubernetes
concepts: Pod stuck Pending? → describe: usually resource constraints, node selectors, or PVC binding
CrashLoopBackOff? → logs: app error. Check previous logs too (kubectl logs -p)
ImagePullBackOff? → registry auth, image name/tag typos, network policy
Systematic order: describe (events) → logs (app) → exec (inside) → node (infra)

example.code:
$ kubectl describe pod x   # EVENTS section is gold
$ kubectl logs x -p         # previous container's logs
$ kubectl exec -it x -- sh  # inside the container
example.walkthrough: Debug a broken deployment using only describe/logs/exec. Document each step and what it revealed.

pitfalls: Deleting and recreating instead of diagnosing — you'll never learn the failure mode
Ignoring events — the scheduler tells you exactly why it's Pending
Debugging the app when it's a platform issue (and vice versa) — check the layer first
lessons.try_it: Create 3 broken pods (bad image, bad port, resource impossible). Diagnose each with the systematic order.

lessons.title: Cloud Core: Compute, Storage, Network
concepts: Compute: VMs (control) vs containers vs serverless (less ops) — match the abstraction to the team's ops capacity
Storage: object (blobs, cheap, infinite), block (disks for VMs), file (shared) — different tools, different bills
Network: VPCs isolate, subnets segment, security groups filter — default-deny, then open deliberately
IAM is the real perimeter: least privilege, roles over users, MFA everywhere — breaches start with overbroad access

example.code:
# least-privilege sketch
# role: deployer → actions: [ecr:Push, ecs:UpdateService]
# resource: arn:...:service/prod-*  (not *)
# condition: MFA present
example.walkthrough: Design a minimal VPC: 2 AZs, public/private subnets, NAT, and security groups for a 2-tier app.

pitfalls: 0.0.0.0/0 ingress 'temporarily' — temporary becomes permanent
One giant IAM role for everything — blast radius of a compromised key
No cost alerts — the $40k surprise bill is a rite of passage you can skip
lessons.try_it: Write an IAM policy for a CI role that can only deploy to staging. Test with the policy simulator.

lessons.title: Terraform: Declarative Infrastructure
concepts: Declarative: you describe the desired state, Terraform figures out the steps — idempotent by design
State files are the source of truth for what's real — protect them (remote backend, locking, no manual edits)
Modules package reusable infrastructure; variables parameterize, outputs expose — DRY for infra
plan before apply, always — the plan is your code review for infrastructure

example.walkthrough: Write Terraform for a VPC + one instance. Run plan, read every line of the diff, then apply.

pitfalls: Local state on a laptop — lost laptop = lost truth; use remote backends
apply without plan review — the infra equivalent of force-push
Hardcoded secrets in .tf files — variables + vault, never plaintext
lessons.try_it: Refactor your config into a module with variables and outputs. Use it twice with different inputs.

lessons.title: Observability: Metrics, Logs, Traces
concepts: Metrics: numbers over time (RED: rate, errors, duration) — alert on symptoms, not causes
Logs: discrete events — structured (JSON) or you're grepping forever; centralize or they don't exist
Traces: follow requests across services — the only sane way to debug microservices latency
SLOs define 'healthy' in user terms; alerts fire on burn rate, not on every blip

example.code:
# RED per service, per endpoint:
# rate(requests_total), errors(5xx), duration(histogram)
# alert: error_rate > 1% for 5m → page
example.walkthrough: Define RED metrics and one SLO for a sample API. Write the alert rule with a runbook link.

pitfalls: Alerting on CPU — users don't care about CPU; alert on error rate and latency
Logs without correlation IDs — can't trace a request across services
Dashboards nobody looks at — if it's not tied to an alert or a ritual, delete it
lessons.try_it: Add structured logging with request IDs to a sample app. Query: show me all logs for one request.

lessons.title: DevOps Projects That Get You Hired
concepts: Hiring managers want: a live pipeline URL, IaC repo, and a README explaining architecture decisions
Project 1: containerized app + CI/CD + IaC-provisioned infra + monitoring — the full loop
Project 2: 'bad to good' — take an insecure/leaky setup and harden it, documenting each fix
Every project needs a 2-minute demo video — text descriptions don't convey running systems

example.code:
Portfolio checklist:
[ ] Live demo URL or video
[ ] IaC repo (Terraform/Ansible)
[ ] Pipeline definition in repo
[ ] README: architecture diagram + decisions
[ ] Monitoring dashboard screenshot
example.walkthrough: Audit your best project against the checklist. Fill the biggest gap this week.

pitfalls: Tutorial clones with zero modifications — interviewers recognize them instantly
No IaC — 'I clicked it up in the console' doesn't demonstrate DevOps
Dead demo links — verify everything the week you apply
lessons.try_it: Record a 2-minute demo of your pipeline: commit → build → deploy → monitor.

lessons.title: DevOps Interview: Troubleshooting Scenarios
concepts: Interviewers simulate incidents: 'deployments are failing' — they watch your systematic approach, not just the answer
Narrate your thinking: 'First I'd check X because...; if that's clean, then Y' — process is the product
Know the layers: is it the app, the container, the orchestrator, the network, or the cloud? Isolate top-down or bottom-up
Always mention verification: 'then I'd confirm with...' — fixes without verification are guesses

example.code:
Scenario: 'Pods keep crash-looping after a deploy.'
Strong: 'describe for events → logs -p for the crash →
  check the image tag actually pushed → verify env/config
  changed → roll back if needed, then root-cause.'
example.walkthrough: Practice 3 troubleshooting scenarios aloud, 5 minutes each. Record and review your narration.

pitfalls: Jumping to the fix before diagnosing — 'just restart it' is not a methodology
Silent debugging — if they can't hear your reasoning, they can't credit it
No rollback mention — production discipline includes knowing when to revert
lessons.try_it: Do a mock troubleshooting round with a peer. Time it. Review where your narration went quiet.

simulations.title: Learn in dependency order
simulations.brief: A career-switcher has spent 3 months on Kubernetes courses but can't use the Linux command line and has never committed to git. Interviews keep stalling at fundamentals. Diagnose the learning order.

steps.symptom: Can describe a Kubernetes Deployment from memory, but can't list files or check disk space on the node.
evidence: 'Couldn't navigate to the log file during the troubleshooting round.'
options: Rebuild from the bottom: Linux fluency, then Git, then containers — each layer makes the next one comprehensible
Double down on Kubernetes — depth in one tool beats breadth
Skip Linux — the cloud console replaces the command line
Learn YAML harder — the interviews are really about YAML
steps.explain: Learn in dependency order: Linux, then Git, then containers, then CI/CD, then cloud and IaC. Skipping layers produces fragile knowledge that collapses the moment an interview goes one level deeper than the tutorial.

steps.symptom: Every new tool feels like starting over — nothing transfers between topics.
evidence: 'Docker networks confuse me. Kubernetes networking confuses me. They feel like different subjects.'
Linux networking: never studied. 'I skipped it to get to containers faster.'
options: The missing Linux networking foundation is why both feel alien — foundations transfer, tools don't
Some people just aren't good at networking — pick a different specialty
Memorize more Docker flags to compensate
Networking doesn't matter for DevOps anymore — it's all managed
steps.explain: Foundations are what transfer. Docker networking and Kubernetes networking are both Linux networking with different wrappers — learn the foundation once and every tool built on it gets easier.

steps.symptom: Three months in, motivation is gone: 'I've learned so much but I can't do anything.'
evidence: 'I can follow along but I freeze when the screen is blank.'
options: Stop consuming tutorials and build one small original project end-to-end — blank-screen ability is the actual skill
Watch tutorials at 2x speed to cover more ground
The field is too hard — consider a different career
Collect more certificates — credentials prove ability
steps.explain: Tutorial fluency is not engineering ability. One original end-to-end project — designed, debugged, and documented by you — builds the blank-screen muscle that interviews actually test.

simulations.debrief: Learn in dependency order — Linux, Git, containers, CI/CD, cloud/IaC — and convert tutorial time into original project time early. Interviews probe what you can do with a blank screen, not what you can recite.

simulations.title: Ten tutorials, zero projects
simulations.brief: A candidate's resume lists 14 completed courses and a portfolio of tutorial clones. In interviews, every answer starts with 'in the tutorial...'. Fix the portfolio.

steps.symptom: Portfolio: 6 projects, all step-by-step clones of popular tutorials, identical to thousands of others.
evidence: Projects: 'Docker course final project', 'K8s tutorial app', 'CI/CD demo' — all from course repos.
'We see this exact project 20 times a week.'
options: Build one original end-to-end project of your own design, with your own decisions documented
Add more tutorial projects — volume shows dedication
Rename the tutorial projects to sound original
Remove the portfolio — courses are enough
steps.explain: One original end-to-end project beats ten tutorials. Interviewers mine debugging stories and decision rationale — tutorial clones have neither, because the decisions were the instructor's.

steps.symptom: Asked 'tell me about a hard bug you fixed', the candidate describes a typo from a tutorial.
evidence: Q: hardest bug? A: 'I misspelled a variable in lesson 7.' Follow-up questions: no depth available.
options: Original projects produce real debugging stories — that's what this question is mining for
Memorize a more impressive bug story
Avoid behavioral questions — focus on technical rounds
The question is unfair to beginners
steps.explain: 'Tell me about a hard bug' is a story prompt, and only real projects generate real stories: the 2 AM deploy, the flaky test, the misconfigured pipeline. Tutorials don't break in interesting ways because the path is paved.

steps.symptom: The candidate can explain CI/CD concepts but has never operated a pipeline they built.
evidence: Skills: Jenkins, GitHub Actions, ArgoCD (all from courses).
Task: 'set up CI for this repo' — stuck at choosing triggers and secrets handling.
options: The pipeline is the product: build and operate CI for your own project until you can whiteboard it for any stack
CI tools are interchangeable — concepts are enough
Let the team handle CI — juniors don't touch pipelines
Watch one more advanced CI course
steps.explain: The pipeline is the core DevOps artifact. Building one — choosing triggers, handling secrets, debugging red builds — is what converts 'I know what CI is' into 'I can ship with it', which is the entire job.

simulations.debrief: Portfolio building is story building: original projects, real debugging, operated pipelines. Interviews don't test what you've watched — they test what you've built and broken.

simulations.title: The failed deploy question
simulations.brief: The interviewer asks: 'Tell me about a time you caused an outage.' The candidate freezes, then says 'I've never broken anything.' The interview ends there. Prepare the story.

steps.symptom: 'I've never broken anything' — intended as a strength, received as inexperience.
evidence: Interviewer: 'Everyone breaks things. I need to know how you respond when you do.'
The candidate once deployed to prod on a Friday; a teammate caught it. Story exists — untold.
options: Prepare real failure stories in STAR format — the question tests ownership and response, not perfection
Maintain the perfect record — admitting faults loses offers
Invent a dramatic outage story to sound experienced
Deflect: 'I prefer to talk about my strengths'
steps.explain: Behavioral interviews test ownership: what happened, what you did, what changed systemically. 'Never broken anything' signals either no real responsibility or no self-awareness — both are red flags for an ops-adjacent role.

steps.symptom: The candidate has a story but tells it as a hero narrative: 'I saved the day at 2 AM.'
evidence: 'I stayed up all night and fixed it myself. The team was asleep.'
Hiring rubric: 'Demonstrates systemic thinking and collaboration under pressure.'
options: Reframe around the systemic fix: what broke, how you responded with the team, and what now prevents recurrence
The hero story is perfect — it shows dedication
Downplay your role to sound humble
Skip the story — heroics are unprofessional
steps.explain: STAR stories for DevOps roles must end with a systemic fix, not just a recovery. 'I fixed it at 2 AM' is a war story; 'we added the check that makes that failure impossible' is an engineering story — interviews hire for the second.

steps.symptom: Asked about conflict with a teammate, the candidate says 'we've always gotten along great.'
evidence: There was a real disagreement about deploy freezes — the candidate avoided the conversation.
options: Use the real disagreement: describe both positions, how you engaged, and what the team decided
Keep saying everything was great — positivity wins
Blame the teammate to show conviction
Say you avoid conflict — it's a strength
steps.explain: DevOps is a culture role as much as a toolchain role: interviews probe how you collaborate and handle disagreement. A real, respectfully-told conflict story beats a flawless-relationships claim every time.

simulations.debrief: Behavioral interviews test ownership: prepare real failure stories in STAR format that end with a systemic fix. The story's value is in the response and the prevention, never in the perfection.

simulations.title: Whiteboard the pipeline
simulations.brief: Final round: 'Whiteboard a CI/CD pipeline for our Python API — from commit to production.' The candidate draws a single box labeled 'Jenkins'. Rescue the round.

steps.symptom: One box labeled 'Jenkins' — no stages, no gates, no environments.
evidence: 'Walk me through what happens when a developer pushes.' — silence.
options: Draw the stages: build, unit test, SAST/scan, artifact publish, deploy to staging, automated tests, gated prod promotion
Add more boxes labeled with tool names — tools are what matter
Jenkins does all of that internally — the diagram is fine
Draw the same single box but bigger
steps.explain: The pipeline is the product: interviewers want stages and decisions, not tool logos. Build, test, scan, publish, stage, verify, promote — each stage is a quality gate, and the diagram should show what each gate checks.

steps.symptom: 'Where do secrets come from in your pipeline?' — the candidate suggests committing them encrypted 'in the repo, it's fine.'
evidence: 'We can encrypt the .env and commit it — developers need it anyway.'
'Who can decrypt it?' — 'Everyone on the team, for velocity.'
options: Secrets come from a secrets manager at runtime; CI gets short-lived scoped credentials — never committed, never shared
Encrypted-in-repo is fine if the key is also in the repo for convenience
Sharing secrets with the whole team is necessary for velocity
Secrets don't matter for a whiteboard exercise
steps.explain: Secret handling is a first-class pipeline design question. Committed secrets — encrypted or not, with shared keys — are a breach waiting for a repo leak. The right answer is manager-backed, short-lived, least-privilege.

steps.symptom: 'How do you roll back a bad production deploy?' — 'We'd fix forward as fast as possible.'
evidence: 'Rollback is admitting defeat — we just push the fix.'
The 'fix' takes 45 minutes to build; users are erroring now.
options: Design for rollback first: immutable artifacts, previous version one promotion away, rollback rehearsed — fix-forward is the backup plan
Fix-forward is the modern way — rollback is legacy thinking
Rollbacks are too risky to attempt
Just scale up the servers until the fix is ready
steps.explain: A pipeline without a rollback path is a hope with YAML. Immutable artifacts mean the last good version is always one step away — that is the primary recovery path; fix-forward is what you do when rollback can't apply.

simulations.debrief: Whiteboard pipelines as stages and gates, not tool names: build, test, scan, publish, stage, verify, promote — with secrets from a manager and rollback designed in from the start.

simulations.title: The salary history trap
simulations.brief: Offer stage: 'What did you make at your last job?' The candidate's last role paid below market. The number they give will anchor everything after it. Navigate the negotiation.

steps.symptom: Recruiter: 'We need your salary history to calibrate the offer.' The candidate's last salary was 30% below market.
evidence: Researched range for the role in this market: $95k-$120k. Last salary: $68k.
options: Decline to share history; anchor on researched market range for the role instead
Share the $68k honestly — honesty is the best policy
Inflate the history number to match the market
Refuse to discuss compensation at all
steps.explain: Negotiate on the role's market value with researched ranges — anchoring to salary history undervalues you, and many jurisdictions restrict those questions. The market rate for the role is the relevant number, not your past.

steps.symptom: The offer comes in at $80k — 'a great raise from your $68k!'
evidence: Offer: $80k. 'That's an 18% raise — most people would be thrilled.'
Same role, same market: $95k-$120k. The offer is below the entire range.
options: Counter with the researched range and your evidence — the raise framing is irrelevant to the role's value
Accept — 18% is a great raise
Accept but keep interviewing secretly
Reject angrily — the lowball is insulting
steps.explain: 'A big raise for you' is anchoring, not generosity. The counter is calm and evidence-based: the role's market range, your qualifications against it, and a specific number. Emotion negotiates nothing; ranges do.

steps.symptom: They won't move on base but mention 'great equity and a bonus'.
evidence: Equity: startup, illiquid, 4-year vest. Bonus: discretionary, 'up to 10%', paid 4% last two years.
Candidate hasn't asked about: on-call burden, title, review cycle, remote policy.
options: Evaluate total compensation honestly and negotiate the non-base terms that matter: title, review cycle, on-call, remote
Equity will make you rich — ignore the base
Bonuses always pay out at target — count the full 10%
Only base salary matters — walk away
steps.explain: Total compensation is base plus the realistic value of everything else — illiquid equity and discretionary bonuses discount heavily. And the negotiable terms beyond money (title, review timing, on-call load) compound over a career.

simulations.debrief: Negotiate on researched market ranges for the role, never on your history. Evaluate the whole offer honestly, counter with evidence, and remember the non-salary terms compound too.

Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix

Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before

Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one

Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened

Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood

Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed

No measurable outcome

No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.
